rows.stake: If shared CLI claims fail, callers can misclassify exits, expose secrets in control records, or publish incorrect report bytes, permissions and success stamps.
If command contract claims fail, machine callers cannot distinguish results from diagnostics or rely on process status before using an output.
If envelope claims fail, a malformed or incompatible structured file can be treated as valid data before its identity is established.
If rendering claims fail, committed documents can silently drift from their inputs or conceal unsupported premises.
If process-wrapper claims fail, child output can be lost or mixed, routing can truncate prior logs, raw arguments can leak, and wrapper statuses can conceal child or delivery failure.
If acceptance claims fail, document stamps can select the wrong reader or turn a refusal into acceptance.
If syntax-tree claims fail, parsed distinctions can disappear before validation or printing.
If CDDL claims fail, schema acceptance can disagree with the declared label language or evaluable subset.
If companion claims fail, an earlier reader can receive a schema with unintended edits.
If document claims fail, malformed envelopes or unsupported values can cross the interchange boundary.
If encoding claims fail, equal values can receive different names or encoded bytes can lose their meaning.
If fragment claims fail, unsupported schema forms can enter algorithms whose guarantees require the assignable fragment.
If inclusion claims fail, incompatible theories can be mistaken for additive refinements.
If label claims fail, identifiers can be parsed ambiguously or accepted outside their canonical language.
If lexical claims fail, invalid input can be tokenized as a different valid schema or diagnostics can identify the wrong position.
If parsing claims fail, schema structure can change or adversarial nesting can cause repeated descent.
If prefix claims fail, incomplete bytes can select a reader prematurely or require more bytes than the declared bound.
If printing claims fail, schema text can change meaning or fail to reach its canonical fixed point.
If sampled metatheorem claims fail, canonical names, bounded routing or compatibility invariants have a concrete counterexample.
If regular-expression claims fail, supported patterns can decide the wrong match or exceed the declared work limit.
If registry claims fail, invalid or ambiguous theory histories can be admitted as supported versions.
If resolution claims fail, names and generic parameters can bind outside their declared scope.
If restraint claims fail, an implicit schema reach can admit forbidden values.
If satisfaction claims fail, a document can receive the wrong schema-conformance verdict.
If theory claims fail, registered schema identity and validation can diverge.
If vector claims fail, interchange behavior disagrees with the independent named conformance cases.
If version claims fail, edition ordering and compatibility can select an unsupported schema.
If correspondence claims fail, changed release fields or lost source pins can be accepted without evidence.
If performance-reporting claims fail, durations can change semantic verdicts or missing observations can be invented.
If build-discipline claims fail, a package, test item or output path can evade the workspace checks.
If harness claims fail, undeclared, missing or misidentified executions can appear as passing evidence.
If identity-citation claims fail, unresolved identities can enter tracked prose or ordinary words can be refused as identities.
If evidence-gate claims fail, missing obligations, unowned claims or failed siblings can be hidden by coverage totals.
If support loses cases, implementation identities or replay inputs, passing tests can conceal a contract failure.
Collapsing parallel identities, admitting partial co-legs or erasing required protocol references changes the complete act set before any domain accounting.
If the outer records witnesses fail, a downstream consumer can accept incomplete acts, miscount causal closure membership or mistake an invalid batch for validated history.
Confusing units, market repricing and recoinage can certify the wrong cost or treat a rounded boundary as exact.
Replacing historical definitions with current constants can change an old boundary answer without changing its identity.
Revaluing a consummated charge at a later price erases its original debit vintage.
Omitted disclosures or repaired marker sets can fabricate readiness, move destruction between addresses, or count one destruction more than once.
If the transport boundary fails, service reachability or credentials can enter public driver state, or an unauthenticated service can supply storage results.
A partial succession, rewritten edition or mixed boundary snapshot can change an earlier verdict or erase the evidence needed to reconstruct it.
Persisting a later edition must not replace the exact constants selected at an earlier boundary.
If public layout decoding drops a field or accepts an ambiguous target, chain evidence can be misattributed or a hostile length can exhaust the reader.
Dropping or duplicating an act across dependent blocks changes the proposed whole-act union and can separate a causal ancestor from its dependent.
An unapproved, incomplete or mis-typed projection can falsely anchor an Actor/Profile pair, while stale mutable graph state can omit or alter accepted records.
A mixed boundary or malformed parameter interpretation can compile a different final state from the accepted public inputs.
If profile claims fail, openings can bind the wrong authored tuple, disclose removable private material or substitute unsupported anchor authority.
